newsitem.title: USA: Dollar slips vs. yen on Japanese rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slips vs. yen on Japanese rate fears.

text.p: The dollar fell against the yen Thursday after a key Japanese central bank official raised the prospect of higher Japanese official interest rates.
Yasuo Matsushita, Governor of the Bank of Japan, told a parliamentary committee that it was important to take pre-emptive policy steps to realise continued growth without inflation.
His remarks helped knock the dollar down to a low of 115.47 Thursday, its weakest level against the yen in more than a week.
Higher rates in Japan would make Japanese assets more attractive, luring investors into yen-denominated securities and thus boosting the Japanese currency.
"The yen strengthened overnight on the comments from Matsushita," said Bob Near, vice president on the corporate foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York.
The dollar stood at 115.72 yen late in New York, down from 116.27 late on Wednesday.
Against other major currencies, however, the dollar was little changed as traders stuck to the sidelines ahead of the widely awaited May employment data, due on Friday.
The dollar ended unchanged at 1.7290 German marks, and up slightly at 1.4455 Swiss francs, compared with 1.4450 late on Wednesday.
The British pound rose to $1.6345 from $1.6332. The dollar ended marginally higher at Canadian $1.3775 against $1.3762.

"The dollar has really been confined to very narrow trading ranges in anticipation of the employment numbers on Friday," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago. "But I think the dollar remains well underpinned because of the turmoil going on in Europe."

French elections last weekend brought in leftist government that has expressed an unwillingness to continue the austerity policies needed for France to meet the strict fiscal criteria for the planned single European currency.

A week-long dispute between the German government and Germany's central bank over Bonn's plans to revalue gold reserves to help it meet the same tough criteria has also sapped investor confidence in Europe's planned single currency.
Both events have led to active selling of marks and other European currencies this week, which has helped the dollar.

A strong employment report on Friday, on top of all the troubles in Europe, could give the dollar the boost it needs to revisit its three-year high of 1.7389 marks, reached in late April, traders said.

"If it comes in near consensus it would confirm nice job creation in stark contrast to what's going on in Germany and could give us enough of a push to challenge ... the highs of the year against the mark," said Bank of New York's Near.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expect May payrolls grew by 219,000 on average.
